title: Simplify or give up: the undeniable lessons of “Don't Make Me Think”
description: The lessons from Steve Krug's Don't Make Me Think, applied to everyday work: clear hierarchy, fewer steps and testing with real people.

related.title: Clint Acquire
related.body: In practice: a landing page and a conversational flow that captured 79% of the sales demand.

blocks.text: Imagine trying to buy a ticket for that can't-miss concert and, instead of clicking through easily, you get lost in menus, endless forms and hidden buttons. Frustrating, right? That's exactly the reality Steve Krug set out to change with the classic Don't Make Me Think. If you're a designer, a developer or simply someone who believes digital doesn't have to be a maze, this article is for you. Get ready to see how simplicity can be your biggest advantage in the digital world.
1. The art of not making the user think
Krug arrived with a bold message: if your design forces the user to think too much, you've already lost points, and possibly sales.

blocks.caption: Visual hierarchy and plain language: the user knows where to click without effort.

blocks.text: Imagine a restaurant where the menu comes with endless explanations of every dish. You'd probably choose something right away from a simple, intuitive menu instead. In the digital world, the same applies: users want to know where to click and what to expect, with no mental effort.

items: Visual hierarchy: Make the essential information stand out clearly. If the user has to decode a message, you've failed.
Plain language: Use words even a non-expert friend would understand, no complicated jargon.

blocks.caption: Same content, different reading: size, contrast and a single primary action tell the user where to look and where to click.

blocks.text: 2. Less is more: a journey without obstacles
Have you noticed that when everything is simplified, the experience feels almost magical? Krug argues that every click, every action, should be as intuitive as turning the page of a good book.

blocks.caption: Every step you remove is one less reason to give up.

blocks.text: Think about an online store. If the checkout has more stages than a reality show, the user will probably give up halfway. Cutting steps, removing unnecessary fields and giving instant feedback are strategies that can boost conversion surprisingly well.

blocks.caption: Fewer fields, one click and an instant response. The user is never left wondering whether it worked.

items: Run a test: ask someone who has never used your site to make a purchase. If they get confused, it's time to rethink the flow!

blocks.text: 3. Test with people, not with your own brain

As a design expert, you may think your solution is obvious, but guess what? What's clear to you can be a riddle to someone else. Krug always stressed the importance of usability testing. It's not about guessing what the user needs, but about watching how they interact with your product.

data.label: 5 people, simple tasks: watch where they get stuck

blocks.caption: The quick test suggested in the article: five people are enough to show where the flow gets stuck.

items: Quick test: Bring in 5 people, ask them to do simple tasks and watch where they get stuck.
Real feedback: The reactions and questions that come up are pure gold for improving your design.

blocks.caption: Watching a task shows what no opinion can: hesitation. When two out of five people get stuck at the same point, that's where the problem is.

blocks.text: At its core, Don't Make Me Think is about creating experiences where the technology disappears and the user feels guided effortlessly. It's almost like having a superpower: turning the complicated into something natural and intuitive.

Remember that famous site that revolutionized the way we search for information? It became a benchmark precisely because it cut out everything unnecessary and focused on what really mattered: delivering results clearly. If even giants like that bet on simplicity, why can't your project shine the same way?

The message is clear: if you want your digital product to be loved, you need to make the user's life easier. It's not about “cutting corners”, but about understanding that every element, every detail, should work to remove barriers, not create them. By adopting the principles of Don't Make Me Think, you not only improve usability, you also win user loyalty and, as a result, stronger business results.

So, ready to turn your designs into experiences that practically sell themselves? Share your stories, challenges and wins in the comments. After all, the best way to learn is, above all, to simplify and share!
